opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the timeline matters a lot here. If AI progress is fast, say we get to systems that can fully automate AI R&D within a few years, then the window for any kind of reversal is pretty short. Once you've automated a large fraction of the work inside AI companies, the competitive pressure to keep it automated is enormous. Going back to humans means you're just way slower than whoever doesn't go back. So in fast-timeline worlds, I'd expect reversals to be rare and mostly local: a particular company pulls back on some deployment because of an incident, but the overall trend keeps going.

In slower-timeline worlds, things look different. If it takes a decade or more for automation to really mature, there's more room for things to go back and forth. You might see a company aggressively automate some function, find that the systems are unreliable or that there are subtle quality problems, and then partially re-hire humans. We've seen versions of this with things like customer service chatbots, where firms over-deploy, get backlash, and pull back somewhat. With slower progress there's more time for regulation, labor pushback, and institutional caution to have an effect.

There's also an important distinction between reversals driven by capability limitations and reversals driven by safety concerns. Capability-driven reversals, where "the AI just isn't good enough yet," become less plausible as systems improve, and in fast timelines that problem resolves itself quickly. Safety-driven reversals, where "we caught the AI doing something sketchy, so we're pulling back," are the ones I think about more. I worry that even when you get a pretty alarming warning shot, like catching a model trying to sabotage research or exfiltrate its weights, the response will be much weaker than people hope. Under short timelines and intense competition, the more likely reaction is "patch it, add some monitoring, keep going" rather than "de-automate and slow down."

So overall: shorter timelines make meaningful reversals less plausible, because the competitive and economic momentum builds so fast. Longer timelines leave more room for course correction, though even then I wouldn't count on it as a default safety mechanism. If we want the option to pull back, I think we need to deliberately build institutions and coordination that make that option actually available, rather than assuming it'll be there when we need it.

r001.rationale: The response says reversals are less plausible on short timelines and that longer timelines leave more room for course correction—the opposite of the criterion.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the timeline question is actually pretty central here, and it cuts in a somewhat non-obvious direction.

If you think we're on a short timeline — say, full automation of AI R&D within something like three to five years — then I think reversals in automation trends become much less plausible, basically because there isn't time for the kinds of things that would cause a reversal to kick in. The way I'd think about it is: what are the mechanisms by which a trend like "AI is doing more and more of the cognitive work" could actually reverse? You've got things like running out of compute, running out of data, hitting some hard algorithmic wall, regulation that actually bites, or maybe a big demand-side shock where companies just stop paying for it. And on a short timeline, most of those just don't have time to materialize before you've already gotten to systems that can substantially accelerate the research itself. And once you're there, the dynamics are pretty self-reinforcing.

Whereas on a longer timeline — if you think this is more like a fifteen- or twenty-year thing — I think reversals become a lot more plausible, and we should put real weight on them. Historically, when you look at other technologies, periods of rapid adoption are often followed by plateaus or even partial retreats. The thing that makes me take that seriously for AI specifically is that a lot of the current trend is being driven by massive capital expenditure that's predicated on expectations about future returns. If those returns are slower to materialize than investors expect, you could easily see a pullback in investment, which slows down compute scaling, which slows down capability progress, and then you get this sort of lull. I don't think that lull would be permanent — the underlying technology still works — but it could look like a reversal for several years.

So one way to summarize my view: the probability of a reversal is kind of inversely related to how fast things are going. The faster the trend, the less time there is for the brakes to engage. And I personally put a decent amount of probability on the shorter timelines, so I end up thinking reversals are less likely than I think a lot of people assume. But I want to be careful here — I'm not saying it's impossible, and I think people who are very confident in continuous exponential progress with no hiccups are also probably overconfident.

The other thing I'd add is that "automation trend" is doing a lot of work in that question. There's the trend in capabilities, and then there's the trend in actual deployment and economic uptake, and those can come apart. I could imagine a world where capabilities keep going up but deployment stalls for a while because of integration difficulties or regulatory friction or just organizational inertia. That looks like a reversal from the outside, but the underlying capability trend hasn't reversed at all. And in that world, you'd expect a kind of catch-up later, where the deployment gap closes quite rapidly once the bottleneck gets removed. So I'd be a bit cautious about reading too much into any apparent slowdown in adoption as evidence that the deeper trend has changed.

r001.rationale: The candidate says reversals are less plausible on short timelines and more plausible on long timelines, the opposite of the criterion.

astra-6.text:
I think the key question is how much time there is for a reversal to happen. If AI goes from automating a relatively small fraction of work to being able to do almost everything in a few years, then there’s much less room for some countervailing trend to become important. You could see a temporary reversal, but the underlying improvement in capabilities could overwhelm it pretty quickly.

If that transition takes decades, then there’s more room for adaptation. People can change what they do, organisations can reorganise, and new kinds of work can become economically important. So I’d be more open to reversals on those timelines. But a longer timeline doesn’t by itself imply a reversal; you still need a mechanism that makes human labour more useful relative to what AI can do.

r001.rationale: The response says reversals are more plausible when the transition takes decades and that short timelines leave less room for them—the opposite of the criterion.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the timeline matters quite a lot. If AI development is slow, you could imagine automating some tasks, then discovering that the remaining tasks are bottlenecked on things humans are particularly good at. And as the economy adjusts, those tasks could become more valuable, so the trend could reverse for a while.

If the transition to much more capable AI happens over just a few years, there’s less time for that adjustment. You might still get temporary reversals in particular occupations, but if AI is rapidly getting better at the tasks that remain, I’d be less inclined to expect a durable reversal in the overall trend. So I’d distinguish a reversal that lasts for a few years from a reason to think humans retain a substantial role indefinitely.

r001.rationale: The response says reversals are more plausible when AI development is slow, and less likely to be durable when development is rapid—the opposite of the criterion.
